title: Take Off Your Engineering Hat
subtitle: On the night of 27 January 1986 a group of engineers said no to a launch. Within hours the recommendation had changed. A case about what it takes to keep a position in a room that wants a yes.

card.who: Thiokol & NASA · the night before Challenger · 1986
card.essence: A recommendation made, challenged, and withdrawn in a single evening. What do people say, and what do they not say, when a position is pushed? Four moves for staying calm and holding it.

intention: you'll analyse a real case of a recommendation that moved under pressure, use four moves to check a challenge and hold a position calmly, and practise doing it out loud.
warmup: Think of a time you changed your mind in a meeting. Was it because of a better argument, or because the room was pushing?
How do you feel when a senior person says, "I'm not convinced"? What do you usually do next?
Is it easier to hold a position by raising your voice or by lowering it? Why?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: The company asked for a five-minute caucus, a private discussion off the call, to talk among themselves.
items.meaning: caucus — a private meeting of a group to decide what position to take.

items.sent: At first it advised against the launch; after the break it reversed its recommendation.
items.meaning: reverse — to change a decision or opinion to the opposite of what it was.

items.sent: Some engineers thought the data was inconclusive: it hinted at a danger but did not prove one.
items.meaning: inconclusive — not leading to a clear or certain result.

items.sent: Who has the burden of proof — the person who says it is unsafe or the person who says it is safe?
items.meaning: burden of proof — the responsibility to show that a claim is true; whoever carries it must convince the others.

vocab.heading: B · Which term means…?
vocab.intro: Three terms: back down · push back · stand your ground. Say the right one, then reveal.

items.sent: Which term means to resist or object to an idea, request or decision?
items.meaning: push back — She pushed back on the deadline. Noun: pushback.

items.sent: Which term means to refuse to change your position under pressure?
items.meaning: stand your ground — Everyone told her to give way, but she stood her ground.

items.sent: Which term means to give up your position or claim in the face of opposition?
items.meaning: back down — He started to object, then backed down.

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.meaning: pressure — the feeling of being pushed to act or decide in a certain way, or the force behind that push.

items.sent: make a ___ for something  ·  a strong ___  ·  in any ___
items.meaning: case — a set of arguments and evidence for a position. "Make the case for" means to argue in support.

items.sent: ___ a decision  ·  the judge ___d the objection  ·  be ___d by the board
items.meaning: overrule — to use authority to reject a decision or opinion that someone else has made.

vocab_use: When did you last have to push back on something at work or in life? How did it go?
What is the difference between standing your ground and being stubborn?
Have you ever been overruled? How did you respond?

story.heading: Part 1 — The night before
paras: On the evening of 27 January 1986, NASA planned to launch the space shuttle Challenger the next morning. The forecast was for an unusually cold night at the launch site in Florida, with temperatures falling well below freezing. The boosters that helped lift the shuttle were built by a company called Morton Thiokol, in Utah.

Some of Thiokol's engineers were worried. Rubber O-rings sealed the joints of the boosters, and on earlier flights the rings had been damaged — more often when the weather was colder. They feared that in the cold the rubber would stiffen and fail to seal. Among them were Roger Boisjoly and Arnie Thompson.

That evening, engineers and managers from Thiokol and NASA held a long telephone conference. The company's first recommendation, presented to NASA, was not to launch at temperatures below 53 degrees Fahrenheit, about 12 degrees Celsius — the temperature of the coldest launch the shuttle had made so far.
checks: What was the forecast, and why did it matter?
What were the engineers afraid of?
What did Thiokol recommend at first?
answers: A very cold night, well below freezing. Cold might stiffen the rubber O-rings that sealed the booster joints.
That the rubber would stiffen and fail to seal the joints in the cold, as had been seen in damage on earlier flights.
Not to launch below 53°F (about 12°C) — the coldest temperature at which the shuttle had launched so far.
story.discuss: The first recommendation was clear and gave a number. What makes a recommendation easier to defend — a number, a reason, or a story?

story.heading: Part 2 — "Next April?"
paras: NASA's managers did not welcome the recommendation. One of them is recorded as saying he was appalled at the reasoning. Another, Lawrence Mulloy, is quoted by several accounts as asking Thiokol: "When do you want me to launch — next April?" He later said he did not believe he was putting pressure on anyone that night.

The engineers' case had a weakness. The data showed damage and cold weather together on some flights, but not all, and the charts they presented did not make the pattern easy to see. Later analysts, including the statistician Edward Tufte, argued that a clearer chart of the whole record would have made the argument much stronger.
Thiokol's managers asked for a few minutes offline. The break, called a caucus, was meant to last five minutes. It took about half an hour.
checks: How did NASA's managers react to the first recommendation?
What was the weakness in the engineers' case?
What did Thiokol ask for, and how long did it last?
answers: With resistance. One said he was appalled; another is recorded asking whether Thiokol wanted to launch "next April".
The data was not clear and their charts did not show the whole pattern; the case was easy to challenge.
A private caucus offline, planned for five minutes, which lasted about half an hour.
story.discuss: "When do you want me to launch — next April?" is not a question; it is a push. How could you answer a line like that calmly?

story.heading: Part 3 — The hat
paras: In the caucus, according to later testimony, a senior Thiokol executive told the company's vice-president for engineering to "take off your engineering hat and put on your management hat". The managers then voted among themselves. When the call resumed, Thiokol reversed its position and recommended that the launch go ahead. NASA accepted.

The next morning, 28 January, Challenger lifted off in very cold weather. Seventy-three seconds later it broke apart and all seven crew members were killed. The presidential commission that investigated found that the joint seal had failed and criticised the decision-making that led to the launch.

People still read the evening in two ways. In one reading, sound engineering advice was overruled by pressure from above and from the customer. In the other, the engineers did not have the clear, convincing data that would have held the room — and silence from those who still had doubts mattered too. Both readings have evidence. The question for anyone who has ever held an unpopular view is what would have made the position hold.
checks: What did the executive tell the vice-president for engineering?
What happened after the call resumed?
What are the two ways people read the evening?
answers: To take off his engineering hat and put on his management hat.
Thiokol reversed its position and recommended launching; NASA accepted. Challenger launched next morning and broke apart after 73 seconds, killing all seven crew.
Either that engineering advice was overruled by pressure — or that the engineers' data was not clear enough to hold the room. Both have evidence behind them.
story.discuss: What would you have needed to hold the position that night — a better chart, a calmer sentence, an ally, or something else?

tool_tab.lead: Pushback tests two things at once: your position and your temperature. People tend to fail in one of two ways — they give way too fast, or they get sharp. The tool has four moves that keep you in the top-right corner of the grid: check the challenge, hold the position, bridge back to your point, and own the gap when you do not know.

cells: SHARP|you hold it, and lose the room
FIRM AND CALM|you hold it, and keep the room
SULKING|you give way, and resent it
SOFT|friendly, but the point is gone

how: Check it. Slow the exchange and make sure you are answering the real question: If I understand correctly, you're asking whether…
Hold it. Acknowledge the challenge, then restate your position with one reason: I hear that, and my recommendation stays the same, because…
Bridge it. If the conversation drifts, bring it back to the point that matters: What matters most here is…
Own the gap. If you do not know, say so and give a date: I don't have that figure to hand. I'll confirm it by Thursday.

sort.intro: Someone has just pushed back on your recommendation. Is each reply too soft, firm and calm, or too sharp? Choose, then check.

items.text: I hear the concern, and my recommendation stands — the risk is small and the saving is real.
items.why: it acknowledges the challenge, restates the position and gives one reason.

items.text: You're probably right. Maybe I haven't thought it through enough.
items.why: it gives the position away before any argument has been made.

items.text: If you had read the report, you wouldn't be asking that.
items.why: it attacks the person instead of answering the question.

items.text: Fine. We'll do it your way, then — and let's see how that goes.
items.why: it sounds like acceptance but it is an accusation; the tone is cold and the position is lost.

items.text: That's a fair challenge. My view hasn't changed, and here is the evidence.
items.why: it respects the challenge and answers it with substance.

items.text: Oh, sorry — I didn't mean to push. Let's forget it.
items.why: apologising for having a view closes the discussion.

items.text: I don't have that figure to hand. I'll confirm it by Thursday.
items.why: it admits the gap without losing authority, and it commits to a date.

breaks: You may be wrong. Holding a position is not the same as refusing to listen. The aim is to change your mind for a good argument, not for a loud one: I'd change my view if I saw…
Weak evidence. Calm tone cannot rescue a thin case. In the story above, a clearer chart might have done more than a firmer voice.
Real danger. When safety, law or ethics are at stake, "firm and calm" may not be enough. You may need to put the concern in writing and take it higher.
discuss: Which of the four moves would be hardest for you under real pressure, and why?
What would make you change your position in a meeting? Say it as a sentence beginning I'd change my view if…

grammar.name: Conceding without giving way
grammar.lead: To hold a position calmly you acknowledge the other view in one clause and keep your own in the next. The grammar of concession does exactly that — and each connector needs a different kind of structure after it.
notes: although / even though + clause: Although the risk is real, it is smaller than the cost of waiting. After although you need a full clause with a subject and verb.
despite / in spite of + noun or -ing: Despite the risk, we recommend going ahead. Despite having doubts, she agreed. Never despite that the…
however / that said + a new sentence: The risk is real. That said, it is smaller than the cost of waiting. These connectors begin a second sentence and are followed by a comma.
unless = if … not: I'd keep my recommendation unless I saw new data. It is a way to show you are open to evidence without giving way to pressure.

exercises.heading: Choose the connector
exercises.intro: Use each word from the box once: although · despite · however · unless.
items: 1. ___ the concern is a fair one, my recommendation has not changed.
2. ___ the pressure from above, she kept her original view.
3. The forecast is cold. ___, no one has shown me data that proves the risk.
4. I won't change the plan ___ you can show me new figures.
answers: 3. However — begins a new sentence, with a comma

exercises.heading: Check and own the gap
exercises.intro: Use each word from the box once: understand · check · hand · confirm.
items: 1. If I ___ correctly, you're asking whether we can finish by Friday.
2. Let me ___ that I've understood the question before I answer.
3. I don't have that figure to ___, but I know where to find it.
4. I'll ___ the number by Thursday and send it to you.

grammar.closing: Now concede one point and hold one: tell me something you accept about a view you disagree with, and then what you still believe.

speak.intro: Check, hold, bridge, own the gap. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “If I understand correctly, you're asking whether…” · “I hear that, and my view stays the same, because…” · “What matters most here is…” · “I don't have that to hand — I'll confirm by…” · “I'd change my view if…”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Two rounds of pushback
paras: Choose one: Argue for or against a four-day working week. Recommend whether a project should go ahead or be cancelled. Explain why a deadline should be moved. Speak for thirty seconds. Then the listener pushes back — That sounds expensive. Why is it worth it? — and you check, hold and stop. Then once more: We tried something similar before and it failed.

tasks.label: Task 2 — Own the gap
paras: The listener asks you a question you cannot answer — a specific figure, a date, a name. Respond in three sentences: what you do not know, what you do know, and when you will confirm it.

tasks.label: Task 3 — The review
paras: Imagine you must brief a committee on the night before Challenger launched. In ninety seconds: what was recommended, what happened to it, and what could have helped it hold. Then answer this challenge: So it was the engineers' fault?

final: "Take off your engineering hat and put on your management hat." When is it right to look at a problem from a different role, and when is it a way of removing responsibility?
Is it fair to ask one person in a room to carry the burden of proof for a safety concern? Who should carry it?
How would you decide, in the moment, whether the person pushing back has a better argument or just more power?
From memory: explain the four moves in four sentences, using although, despite, unless and I don't have that to hand.

practice.intro: One page of challenges for using the Calm Hold again and again. Your partner reads a challenge aloud. You check it, hold your position with one reason, bridge back to what matters, or own the gap if you do not know. Keep your voice warm and your position steady.
steps: Check: make sure you have understood. If I understand correctly, you're asking whether…
Hold: acknowledge, then restate with one reason. I hear that, and my view stays the same, because…
Bridge: bring it back. What matters most here is…
Own the gap: if you do not know, say so and give a date.

groups.title: About cost and money
groups.intro: Someone says your idea is too expensive.
questions: That is far too expensive. Why should we pay that?
Your competitor is half your price. Why not match it?
We do not have the budget for this. What else can you do?
Can you take twenty per cent off?
Why is it more expensive than last year?
I do not see the return. Convince me.

groups.title: About your numbers and evidence
groups.intro: The challenge is to your facts.
questions: Where did you get that figure?
I do not believe those numbers.
That survey is too small to mean anything.
Is that a fact or an opinion?
Last quarter you said something different.
Have you checked this with anyone else?

groups.title: From someone senior
questions: I have been doing this for twenty years, and that will not work.
I think you are wrong. Change it.
We have already decided. Why are you raising this now?
Just do it the way I asked.
Why are you making this difficult?
I do not have time for this. Give me a yes or a no.

groups.title: From a colleague or a client
groups.intro: The pressure is personal, so the voice matters.
questions: You are overreacting.
That is not what we agreed.
You are being too negative.
Everyone else is happy with the plan. What is your problem?
Can you just sign it off? It is only a formality.
That is not my job.

groups.title: Everyday pushback
groups.intro: Low stakes, a good place to build the habit.
questions: Why should I pay for the damaged one?
Come on, have another drink, everyone else is.
You always say no to everything.
Why do you not like my idea?
Why do you get to choose the film?
You are being stubborn.

groups.title: When you do not know
groups.intro: Own the gap, and give a date.
questions: What is the exact figure for last quarter?
How many customers have complained?
What does the contract say about this?
When will it actually be finished?
How does this compare with the other region?
What is the legal position?

models.q: That is far too expensive. Why should we pay that?
parts: If I understand correctly, you are asking why the price is higher than you expected.
I hear that, and my recommendation stays the same, because the price includes support after the launch.
What matters most is that you do not have a second bill in month three.

models.q: I do not believe those numbers.
parts: You are asking where the figures come from, and whether they can be trusted?
They come from our own records for the last twelve months, and I am confident in them.
The one I cannot confirm is the regional split. I will check that and send it to you by Thursday.
I hear that it feels that way to you.
I am calm. What I am saying is that the date is not realistic, and here is why.
What I want is a plan we can all keep to.

models.q: Just do it the way I asked.
parts: If I understand correctly, you want it done by the end of the week, in the original format.
I can do that, and I want to be clear that I think the second format is safer, because the client will see the figures sooner.
What matters most is that you are comfortable when it goes out. Which would you like?
I am not a lawyer, and I do not want to guess.
What I can tell you is what the contract says about the timing.
I will ask our legal team and come back to you by Friday.

models.q: Come on, have another drink, everyone else is.
parts: I am fine with this one, because I have an early start.
Let us decide where we are eating.

practice.models_intro: Six examples. Try answering the challenge first, then open the answer to see how the moves fit together.
harder: Second push: your partner repeats the challenge, louder. Hold the same position in different words, without getting sharper.
Concede a little: find one thing the other person is right about, say it, and still hold your main point.
Change your mind: your partner gives you a real new fact. Say what would change your view, and then change it, cleanly.
Written reply: answer the same challenge in a short email. Keep the same order.
Different tone: answer as if you were tired, then as if you were warm. Which version holds better?
